canonical_statement: The primary objective was to evaluate existing evidence for the protective effect of probiotics against antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in adults.
Secondary objectives were to examine dose-response and species-specific response in preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials of adults receiving antibiotics that compared a probiotic regimen with placebo, an alternative probiotic dose or strain, or no treatment for prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

population.label: Adults receiving antibiotic therapy
inclusion_criteria: Adult population receiving any antibiotic therapy for any reason or course length
exclusion_criteria: Probiotics used only to treat established antibiotic-associated diarrhoea

canonical_statement: The review was limited to studies written in English.
The intervention was probiotic therapy of any strain, dose, or formulation given for prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.
Eligible comparators were placebo, an alternative probiotic dose, an alternative probiotic strain, or no treatment.

concept.text: Placebo / alternative probiotic regimen / no treatment

canonical_statement: The primary outcome was incidence of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea as defined by each study during antibiotic treatment or follow-up.

outcome.definition: Incidence of AAD as defined by study authors during antibiotic treatment or follow-up

canonical_statement: The authors performed an electronic title search of CINAHL Plus, EMBASE, MEDLINE (Ovid), Web of Science, and Google Scholar from database inception through May 2021.
Grey literature and trial registries, including ClinicalTrials.gov and ANZCTR, were searched, and reference lists of relevant systematic reviews and included studies were hand searched.
Two of three authors independently assessed each study for inclusion, with discrepancies resolved through discussion.
Data were extracted by two of three authors using a standardized extraction form following PRISMA and housed in Covidence.
Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool across sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other bias domains.
Overall evidence quality was rated using the GRADE approach by two authors with consensus discussion.

All meta-analyses used random-effects models; dichotomous outcomes were reported as risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals, with I-squared used for statistical heterogeneity and NNT calculated for the complete-case analysis.

A priori heterogeneity variables included probiotic dose, probiotic species, and risk of bias; post hoc subgroup analyses evaluated baseline AAD risk and concurrent probiotic use with H. pylori eradication.
The supplemental protocol specified adults aged 18 years or older, any inpatient or outpatient setting, RCTs only, and the same primary prevention outcome.

The supplemental search strategy used title-field terms for population, probiotic intervention, comparator, and diarrhoea outcomes and listed CINAHL Plus, EMBASE, MEDLINE, Web of Science, Google Scholar, registries, and reference-list searching.
Forty-two randomized controlled trials with 11,305 participants were included; the reported overall age range was 15 to 85 years.

The PRISMA diagram shows 352 records from database searching plus 4 additional records, 250 records after duplicate removal, 60 full-text articles assessed, and 42 studies included in qualitative and quantitative synthesis.
Of the 42 included trials, 33 were placebo controlled and eight used no treatment as a comparator; one trial included both placebo and no-treatment controls.
Six of 42 included studies were rated low risk of bias and 36 were rated high or unclear risk of bias.
Across 42 studies and 11,305 participants, probiotics reduced antibiotic-associated diarrhoea versus any control (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.73; p<0.00001).

canonical_statement: Thirty-two of 42 included studies reported adverse events; no serious adverse events were reported in those studies.
One included study reported four non-serious adverse events (2.0%) in the probiotic group versus none in control, and another reported poorer tolerance of probiotic milk than placebo milk.
The funnel plot for the complete-case analysis was visually symmetrical, which the authors interpreted as little evidence of publication bias.
Using GRADE, the authors rated the overall quality of evidence as moderate, citing design limitations but a good effect magnitude and a dose-response gradient.

There was substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity across studies, including probiotic species, dose, formulation, timing, populations, antibiotics, and AAD definitions; overall statistical heterogeneity was I²=60%.
The review measured only incidence of diarrhoea and did not synthesize duration or severity of AAD, hospitalisation due to diarrhoea, or quality-of-life outcomes.
Subgroup analysis by antibiotic was not possible because many studies did not report antibiotic name, class, route, dose, or course length.
The review included only English-language studies and used a title search rather than a keyword search, which the authors noted may have reduced study identification.
The authors concluded that probiotics provide a moderate protective effect against AAD, with an NNT of 20, but cautioned that the overall estimate may not apply when baseline AAD risk is low.
The authors suggested that doses greater than 10 billion colony-forming units per day may be more effective, based on the four studies directly comparing higher and lower doses of the same probiotic.
The authors highlighted L. acidophilus, L. casei, and S. boulardii as having moderate protective effects across more trials than species with larger point estimates but sparse evidence.
